title: Foraging rosehips for syrup and tea
subtitle: Harvest, the seed-hair hazard, and preparation
excerpt: Rosehips are the red or orange fruits of wild roses ripening in UK hedgerows from August through December. They make a deep-pink syrup and a fruity tea. Strain carefully: the seeds inside carry tiny hairs that need to be removed before eating.
sourceNotes: Richard Mabey, Food for Free (1972); John Wright, The Forager's Calendar (2019); BSBI species accounts for Rosa canina; Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981.

glossaryTerms.definition: Matching three independent visual, scent, or habitat features before eating any wild plant. All three must match; a single mismatch means stop.
A wild plant that resembles an edible species closely enough to cause misidentification. Many look-alikes are toxic.

content.text: Rosehips are the oval or round red or orange fruits of wild rose species (Rosa canina and close relatives) ripening in UK hedgerows from August through December. They make a deep-pink syrup rich in vitamin C, a fruity tea, and a sharp jelly. Strain the cooked pulp carefully through a cloth or fine strainer before use: the seeds inside are covered in tiny stiff hairs that cause irritation if swallowed whole. Verify your identification before eating; if in doubt, do not eat.
Apply the
rule-of-three identification

: confirm (1) the oval or round red or orange fruit with a crown of dried sepals at the tip, (2) the arching, thorny stem with pinnate compound leaves of five to seven leaflets, and (3) the hedgerow or scrubland habitat. All three must match.
ID features
Fruit: oval or round, 1 to 3 cm, red through orange when ripe. A crown of dried sepals at the tip (the withered flower parts). Single large seeds inside surrounded by small stiff hairs.
Stems: arching, thorny, with curved or hooked thorns. Stems turn from green to red as they age.
Leaves: pinnate, five to seven oval leaflets with toothed edges. Dog rose (Rosa canina) is the most common UK species.
Flower (May to July): five pink or white petals. Single flowers, not clustered. Appears before the fruit.
Poisonous look-alikes
Rosehip has few toxic UK
look-alike plants
in its fruiting form; the sepal crown and thorny stem make it fairly distinctive. Check for:
Hawthorn haws: similarly red and small but round, slightly waxy, without the sepal crown, on a thorny shrub with lobed (not pinnate) leaves.
When and how to harvest

Pick from August through December. Hips are best after the first frosts when they turn a darker red and the flesh softens. Firm red hips picked in October are also usable for syrup. Snap or snip individual hips from the stem. Avoid ground-level hips on dog-walked paths.
After harvesting

For syrup: top and tail the hips with scissors, halve them, and scoop out the seeds and hairs with a small spoon. Alternatively simmer whole, mash, and strain twice through a double layer of muslin or a fine-mesh strainer, pressing the pulp through while holding the cloth. Strain at least twice; the hairs are too small to see easily. For tea: dry the whole hips, then crush them and steep in hot water before straining.
Legal and ethical

The Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 and Theft Act 1968 allow collection of fruit from hedgerows and common land for personal use. Private land requires the landowner's permission. Leave at least a third of the hips on each plant for birds, especially in hard winters when rosehips are a key food source.

rows.symptom: Throat or mouth irritation after eating rosehip products
rows.cause: Seed hairs not fully removed during straining
rows.fix: Strain the syrup or puree at least twice through a fine cloth or fine-mesh strainer. A double layer of muslin works well. The irritation passes within a few minutes.

rows.symptom: Syrup is very thin even after simmering
rows.cause: Too much water added, or hips were very ripe and soft
rows.fix: Simmer longer to reduce, or add a little sugar and reduce more firmly. Rosehip syrup thickens as it cools.
